name: Incident Response Common Pitfalls
description: This module lists the most common pitfalls encountered in incident response work, so they can be actively avoided rather than rediscovered.
content:
This module lists the most common pitfalls encountered in incident response work, so they can be actively avoided rather than rediscovered.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. State assumptions about incident response explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
2. Keep incident response changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
3. Measure before optimizing any incident response bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
4. Surface known limitations of a chosen incident response approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
5. When incident response decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
6. When multiple incident response strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
7. Prefer explicit, readable incident response solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
8. Re-check edge cases relevant to incident response (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
9. When incident response guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
10. Before starting incident response work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
11. Validate incident response outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
12. Prefer the simplest incident response approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not silently drop incident response edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Do not apply generic incident response advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not skip documenting incident response assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for incident response, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
